title: Documentation, medical necessity and accurate billing
summary: Payers, including Medicare and Medicaid, pay for services that are medically necessary and documented. Records should show the assessment behind the diagnosis, how symptoms affect daily life, a plan with measurable goals, what was done in each session, progress, and why care continues. Codes and diagnoses must reflect what actually happened; choosing them to fit coverage is fraud. This page is information, not legal advice.
keyPoints: Medical necessity documentation usually links the diagnosis, functional impairment, goals, interventions and progress. Plan review frequency is set by payers and state Medicaid programs, not by one federal rule.
Time-based psychotherapy codes depend on time actually spent, so record start and stop times or total time. Code descriptors are copyrighted by the AMA; use your payer's current coding guidance.
Crisis psychotherapy codes and the interactive complexity add-on have specific qualifying conditions. Using an interpreter alone does not qualify for interactive complexity.

Report diagnoses, services and fees accurately (APA Standard 6.06). Up-coding, billing for services not provided, or choosing a diagnosis to get coverage can violate the False Claims Act for federal programs.
Z codes describe social factors such as housing or relationship problems; CMS encourages recording them when assessed.
Auditors can request progress notes. Psychotherapy notes kept separately are not needed for billing and have extra protection.
Mental health parity laws limit stricter coverage rules for mental health than for medical care; enforcement of parts of the 2024 parity rule was paused in 2025, so check current status.
whatToDo: Write each note so it shows the service, time, intervention, client response and how it ties to the plan.
Review and update the plan on the schedule your payers require, with the client.
Choose codes and diagnoses only from what you assessed and did, and fix errors promptly.
Keep a copy of current payer documentation rules, and audit a sample of your own notes each year.
Consult a healthcare attorney or billing compliance adviser, and your licensing board, about coding and documentation questions.

appPositioning: The app never assigns a diagnosis or states a final one. ICD codes appear as references for clinician review, and plan and note exports are drafts the clinician edits and signs in their own record system.
